    <script>
    // Two things the audio-slideshow plugin needs help with.
    //
    // 1. It assigns <source>.src AFTER the <audio> is in the DOM.  Per spec
    //    that does not start a fetch -- the browser only ever issues the
    //    plugin's HEAD probe, never a GET, so the clip never loads
    //    (networkState stays LOADING, duration null) and the deck is silent
    //    or stutters.  Calling load() on the element fixes it.
    //
    // 2. Browsers refuse to start audio until the page has had a real user
    //    gesture, so autoplay:true alone leaves slide 1 silent.  One click
    //    on the overlay satisfies that; after it the plugin runs itself.
    (function () {
      function playerFor(h, v) {
        return document.getElementById('audioplayer-' + h + '.' + v);
      }
      function prime(a) {
        if (!a) return;
        if (a.readyState === 0) { try { a.load(); } catch (e) {} }
      }
      function currentPlayer() {
        var i = (window.Reveal && Reveal.getIndices) ? Reveal.getIndices()
                                                     : { h: 0, v: 0 };
        return playerFor(i.h, i.v || 0);
      }
      function start() {
        var a = currentPlayer();
        prime(a);
        if (a) { var pr = a.play(); if (pr && pr.catch) pr.catch(function () {}); }
      }
      function arm() {
        if (window.Reveal && Reveal.on) {
          Reveal.on('slidechanged', function () { prime(currentPlayer()); });
        }
        prime(currentPlayer());
        if (document.getElementById('audio-start')) return;
        var d = document.createElement('div');
        d.id = 'audio-start';
        d.innerHTML = '<button style="font: 600 22px/1 Calibri, sans-serif;' +
          'color:#fff;background:#b40000;border:0;border-radius:6px;' +
          'padding:18px 30px;cursor:pointer">&#9654;&nbsp; Play with narration</button>' +
          '<div style="margin-top:14px;font:16px Calibri,sans-serif;color:#17375d">' +
          'your browser needs one click before it will play audio</div>';
        d.style.cssText = 'position:fixed;inset:0;z-index:60;display:flex;' +
          'flex-direction:column;align-items:center;justify-content:center;' +
          'background:rgba(255,255,255,.92);text-align:center';
        d.addEventListener('click', function () { start(); d.remove(); });
        document.body.appendChild(d);
      }
      // Narration is generated separately (see the presentation-narration
      // skill).  Until audio/slide0.0.mp3 exists, skip the overlay entirely
      // rather than offer a Play button that plays nothing.
      function armIfNarrated() {
        fetch('audio/slide0.0.mp3', { method: 'HEAD' })
          .then(function (r) { if (r.ok) arm(); })
          .catch(function () {});
      }
      if (document.readyState === 'loading') {
        document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', armIfNarrated);
      } else { armIfNarrated(); }
    })();
    </script>

This is nlmixr2 bayes. A Stan interface for nlmixr2 -- and, as
the hex says, powered with Stan rather than replacing it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three things I will talk about today

First, how nlmixr2 bayes works

Second, what that buys you.

And third, how we checked that it is right.
:::

## 1. Link the likelihood, don't translate the model {.sectionbreak}

![](images/sec-link.jpg){.nostretch}

::: {.notes}
So let's start with what the package actually does.
:::

## Until now, going Bayesian meant maintaining the model twice


::: {.notes}
Can you do Bayesian estimation? This is a common question I get.

Until now the answer was not yet.  For now you have to write it again in Stan. Hand
code the model with Torsten, or if you have NONMEM move it over to NONMEM's bayes
methods.

Either way you end up maintaining two models. The nlmixr2 one, and the Stan one.

And when those two disagree, you had to figure out why.
:::

## Stan does not need your model -- it needs your likelihood

```{=html}
<svg class="dg" viewBox="0 0 1000 430" role="img"
     aria-label="One nlmixr2 model feeds a single shared likelihood layer: rxode2 solves the ODEs and handles the dosing events, and nlmixr2est evaluates the conditional log-likelihood and its analytic gradients. focei, saem and agq draw on that layer directly. Stan reaches the same layer through an external function boundary, receiving the log-likelihood value and its analytic gradient, and supplies the priors and the NUTS sampler on its own side.">
  <rect x="330" y="20" width="340" height="56" rx="8" fill="#eef3f9" stroke="#1f497d" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text class="lab blue" x="500" y="45" text-anchor="middle">your nlmixr2 model</text>
  <text class="sm" x="500" y="66" text-anchor="middle">one function, plus prior() lines in ini({})</text>

  <line x1="500" y1="78" x2="500" y2="108" stroke="#6b7b90" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a2)"/>

  <rect x="60" y="112" width="880" height="118" rx="8" fill="#f2f7ea" stroke="#4a7d18" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <text class="lab grn" x="500" y="137" text-anchor="middle">one compiled likelihood</text>
  <rect x="90" y="152" width="390" height="60" rx="6" fill="#fff" stroke="#4a7d18" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text class="t" x="285" y="176" text-anchor="middle">rxode2</text>
  <text class="sm" x="285" y="198" text-anchor="middle">ODE solve &#183; dosing events &#183; sensitivities</text>
  <rect x="520" y="152" width="390" height="60" rx="6" fill="#fff" stroke="#4a7d18" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text class="t" x="715" y="176" text-anchor="middle">nlmixr2est</text>
  <text class="sm" x="715" y="198" text-anchor="middle">conditional log-lik &#183; analytic gradients</text>

  <g stroke="#6b7b90" stroke-width="2" fill="none">
    <path d="M180,236 L180,286" marker-end="url(#a2)"/>
    <path d="M820,236 L820,286" marker-end="url(#a2)"/>
  </g>

  <rect x="40" y="292" width="280" height="56" rx="6" fill="#fff" stroke="#6b7b90" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text class="t" x="180" y="316" text-anchor="middle">focei &#183; saem &#183; agq</text>
  <text class="sm" x="180" y="338" text-anchor="middle">unchanged</text>

  <rect x="680" y="292" width="280" height="86" rx="6" fill="#f7eeee" stroke="#b40000" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <text class="t red" x="820" y="316" text-anchor="middle">Stan &#183; NUTS</text>
  <text class="sm" x="820" y="338" text-anchor="middle">priors, the eta hierarchy,</text>
  <text class="sm" x="820" y="358" text-anchor="middle">and the sampler</text>

  <line x1="640" y1="262" x2="1000" y2="262" stroke="#b40000" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text class="sm red" x="820" y="256" text-anchor="middle">external function boundary: value + analytic gradient</text>

  <text class="sm" x="330" y="404" text-anchor="middle">The Stan program never sees the ODE system --</text>
  <text class="sm" x="330" y="424" text-anchor="middle">so anything rxode2 can solve is in scope without the generator knowing about it.</text>

  <defs>
    <marker id="a2" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#6b7b90"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
</svg>
```

::: {.notes}
Here is the idea the whole package rests on.

Stan does not actually need your model. It needs a log density and a
gradient.

So rather than translate the model into Stan's language, we link Stan
to the likelihood that already exists. We keep our own
ODE solving and dose handling and individual likelihoods.
Stan calls the compiled model as an external function, and gets the
analytic gradients handed to it.

Stan still owns the parts that are genuinely Bayesian -- the priors,
the eta hierarchy, and the sampler itself.

One model. One likelihood. One source of truth.
:::

## Priors are declared next to the parameters they describe

```r
one.cmt <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- 0.45
    tcl <- log(c(0, 2.7, 100))
    tv <- 3.45
    add.sd <- c(0, 0.7)
    eta.ka ~ 0.6; eta.cl ~ 0.3; eta.v ~ 0.1
    prior(tka) ~ dnorm(0.45, 1)
    prior(tcl) ~ dnorm(1, 1)
    prior(tv) ~ dnorm(3.45, 1)
    prior(add.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 2.5)
  })
  model({ ... })
}
```

::: {.smaller}
All 39 real-valued distributions in the `lotri` catalog -- and the
catalog is deliberately one-to-one with Stan's, so `dcauchy()` means
what Stan means by it. `lotri::lotriPriorDists()` lists them.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the standard toy model with the four new prior lines.

Priors are right next to the parameters they describe, in the same
syntax as everything else in the initialization block.

The distribution catalog is deliberately one to one with Stan's -- all
thirty nine real valued distributions.

:::

## `est="nuts"` gives back an ordinary [nlmixr2]{.nlmixr} fit

```r
fit <- nlmixr2(one.cmt, theo_sd, est="nuts",
               control=nutsControl(seed=42, chains=2, iter=1000))
```

::: rule
:::

```r
print(fit)
#> -- nlmixr2 Stan (HMC) (2 chains x 500 draws; max Rhat 1.009; min ESS 377) --
#>         Est.     SE %RSE Back-transformed(95%CI) BSV(CV%) Shrink(SD)%
#> tka    0.469  0.222 47.4       1.60 (1.03, 2.47)     92.9       17.1
#> tcl     1.01  0.103 10.2       2.75 (2.24, 3.36)     32.8       20.4
#> tv      3.45 0.0524 1.52       31.5 (28.5, 35.0)     17.2       26.1
#> add.sd 0.707 0.0544 7.69    0.707 (0.601, 0.814)
```

::: {.smaller}
`"nuts"` names the *algorithm*, the way `"foce"` and `"focei"` do --
IPRED, CWRES, `plot(fit)` and the rest work, because the fit object
does not know Stan produced the numbers.
:::

::: {.notes}
Fitting is one call. The estimation method is nuts.

Nuts names the algorithm -- Stan's no U turn sampler -- rather than the
software tool.

And what comes back is an ordinary nlmixr2 fit object. The sampler
diagnostics are in the header, the posterior is summarized in the
usual par fixed table with all the other features of a nlmixr2 fit
:::

## A model with no priors is refused -- and the error is the fix

```r
nlmixr2(noPriors, theo_sd, est="nuts")
#> Error: no priors declared; add prior() lines to ini({}), e.g.
#>   prior(tka) ~ dnorm(0.45, 1)
#>   prior(tcl) ~ dnorm(0.993, 1)
#>   prior(tv) ~ dnorm(3.45, 1)
#>   prior(add.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 2.5)
```

::: rule
:::

Bayesian output built on silently-invented priors looks every bit as
publishable as the real thing, and is wrong.

The one default is on `omega` blocks -- `lkj_corr_cholesky(2)` on the
correlation, half-Cauchy on each SD -- and even that is *announced* in a
message rather than assumed quietly.

::: {.notes}
Note that a model with no priors errors.

However, the error message suggests prior lines to put in your
initialization block, derived from the model's own starting values and
bounds.

The one place we do supply a default is on the omega blocks which will
be announced when running the fit
:::

::: {.notes}
Now, what does linking Stan to nlmixr2 actually buy you?

## Stan's ODE interface cannot express a dose

```{=html}

  <line x1="120" y1="325" x2="180" y2="325" stroke="#b40000" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a3)"/>

  <defs>
    <marker id="a3" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto">

</svg>
```

::: {.notes}

This provides dose handling for pharmacometrics datasets.  No more hand-coding
 stan.  Not only that, it is
tested by everything that our package has been using for years

:::

## Delay differential equations are ordinary models here

```r
model({
  ...
  d/dt(R) <- kin - kout * delay(R, tau)   # tau is estimated like any theta
})
```

::: rule
:::

::: checks
- Stan has **no DDE solver at all** -- and never needs one, because it
  never sees the ODE system
- `rxode2` switches to a dense solver behind the likelihood, exactly as
  it does under `focei` or `saem`
- The same is true of M2/M3/M4 censoring, the residual-error catalog,
  `linCmt()` closed forms, mu-referenced covariates and estimated
  `boxCox()` lambda
:::

::: {.notes}

One of the other consequences is that if you have a new feature in nlmixr2 it is inherited in stan.

For example, the new delay differential equations can now be expressed
in stan with this linkage, something you couldn't do in stan at all
without this linkage.

The same argument covers the censoring machinery, the residual error
catalog, and the closed form solved  solutions. None of that needed
special handling on the Stan side. It was already in the likelihood.
:::

## Linked, the same model draws 2.4x more effective samples per second

::: bigtable
|                        | native Stan | nlmixr2bayes (linked) |
|------------------------|-------------|-----------------------|
| wall clock             | 142.7 s     | **80.8 s**            |
| worst bulk ESS         | 236         | **286-378**           |
| **worst ESS / s**      | 1.66        | **4.04**              |
| gradient evaluation    | 1.98 ms     | 1.36 ms (C level)     |
| posterior means        | agree to < 0.01 on every parameter ||
:::

::: {.smaller}
Three things get it there: chains run in **forked processes** (draws
bit-identical to a sequential run); the whole gradient comes from **one
solve per subject**; and `Omega^-1` is rebuilt on the C side
instead of by evaluating an R closure every single evaluation.
:::

::: {.notes}
I did not expect this result, so let me be clear about what is being
compared. This is the same model, with the same priors, fitted two
ways: once as a hand written native Stan program, and once linked.

The posterior means agree to better than a hundredth on every
parameter. So we are comparing two routes to the same answer.

The linked run is about twice as fast in wall clock, and -- more
importantly -- it extracts more effective samples per draw. Put
together, that is two point four times the effective samples per
second.

Three things got it there. The chains run in forked processes, and
those draws are bit identical to a sequential run.
:::

## Parallelism has two axes, and neither one is Stan's threading

```{=html}

On the right, with chainCores set to one, the chains run sequentially and each single likelihood evaluation is split across OpenMP threads by subject.">
  <text class="lab blue" x="250" y="42" text-anchor="middle">default: forked chains</text>

  </g>

  <text class="lab blue" x="750" y="42" text-anchor="middle">chainCores = 1: threads inside</text>
  <text class="mono" x="750" y="66" text-anchor="middle">stanControl(cores=)</text>

    <text x="643" y="172" text-anchor="middle">subj</text>

  <text class="sm grn" x="750" y="322" text-anchor="middle">every single evaluation</text>

  <text class="sm" x="500" y="366" text-anchor="middle">The ODE solve is the rate-limiting step either way -- so that is where the cores go.</text>
</svg>
```

::: {.notes}
A word on parallelism, because it works differently here.

We deliberately do not engage Stan's threading. Layering Stan's
threading runtime on top of our own would just have the two of them
contend with each other for the same cores.

So there are two axes instead. By default, on unix, the chains run in
forked processes.

Or, if you set chain cores to one, the chains run sequentially and each
individual likelihood evaluation is split across threads by subject
instead.

Either way the O-D-E solve is the rate limiting step in a
pharmacometric model, so that is where the cores go.
:::

## ADVI and Pathfinder are the fast first look, not the answer

```r
fitAdvi <- nlmixr2(one.cmt, theo_sd, adviControl(seed=42))
fitPf   <- nlmixr2(one.cmt, theo_sd, pathfinderControl(seed=42))
```

::: rule
:::

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Same generated program, same linked likelihood
- 3-10x faster; ADVI about 30-40 s, Pathfinder about 90 s here
- Passing the control **is** the `est=`, the way `foceControl()` implies
  `est="foce"`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- ADVI understates tails and posterior correlations
- Pareto k-hat replaces Rhat and ESS on those fits
- k-hat above 0.7 warns; hierarchical PK posteriors routinely exceed it
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The same generated program and the same linked likelihood also run
Stan's variational approximations, and multi path Pathfinder.

Each one has its own control object and each runs a separate estimation routine.

These are three to ten times faster. On this model, add vee finishes in
about thirty to forty seconds.

But add vee is an approximation, and it understates tails and
posterior correlations. So treat these two as the fast first look, and
treat NUTS as the answer.
:::

## The posterior is right there, and so is the `stanfit`

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```r
fit$posteriorSummary   # exact quantiles
fit$objDf              # FOCEi, WAIC, LOO rows
fit$stanCode           # the generated program
sf <- fit$stanfit      # rstan::stanfit
rstan::traceplot(sf, pars="tka")
bayesplot::mcmc_pairs(sf, ...)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .checks}
- `$parFixed` CIs are a **Wald** approximation -- for SDs and small
  omegas quote the exact quantiles instead
- WAIC and LOO are **leave-one-subject-out**: the subject is the
  exchangeable unit
- Declared Stan parameters read like your model -- `tka`, `add_sd`,
  `sd_eta_ka`
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Beyond the usual accessors, the fit carries the posterior itself.

Two things worth knowing. The confidence intervals are a Wald
approximation built from the posterior covariance, so for anything
skewed -- standard deviations, small omegas -- you want the exact
quantiles from posterior summary instead.

And the typical bayesian statistics are leave one subject out, not leave one
observation out, because the subject is the exchangeable unit of a
hierarchical model.

The whole R Stan fit object is kept, so trace plots, bayesplot,
posterior, and the rest of that ecosystem all work unchanged.

:::

## 3. Is it right? {.sectionbreak}

![](images/sec-right.jpg){.nostretch}

::: {.notes}
Which brings me to the validation section
:::

## Every claim is checked against something that shares no code with it

::: bigtable
| check | agreement |
|---|---|
| Stan's assembled gradient vs. Richardson finite differences | ~3e-8 |
| `d/d(eta)`, `d/d(theta)` vs. central differences of the conditional | ~3e-8 |
| quadrature marginal vs. `est="agq"` at nAGQ=101 | 3e-7 |
| censored M2/M3/M4 and `ll()` vs. hand-computed textbook densities | exact |
| prior-only sampling vs. every declared prior | one-sample KS each |
| full posterior vs. a hand-written **native-Stan** implementation | within 3x MCSE |
| the linked likelihood engine itself | NONMEM-validated upstream |
:::

::: {.notes}
Because the bridge works at the likelihood level, the checks have to be
at the likelihood level too.

These are the independent ones -- each is a check against something the
bridge shares no code with.

And underneath all of it, the linked likelihood engine is the one
already validated against NONMEM upstream in nlmixr2.
:::

## What is in scope is stated, and everything else is refused

:::: columns
::: {.column width="55%" .checks}
- mixed **and** population-only (single-subject) models
- ODE, DDE and `linCmt()`
- censoring, the residual catalog, user `ll()` endpoints
- mu-referenced and non-mu etas; mu-referenced covariates, fixed or
  time-varying
- estimated `alag`/`f`/`dur`/`rate`, estimated Box-Cox lambda, IOV,
  2-component `mix()`
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Refused with an explanation**

- mixtures beyond two components, for now


- the 8 discrete distributions

::: rule
:::

Deliberately first-order: no Riemannian HMC, no embedded Laplace. NUTS,
ADVI, Pathfinder and optimization are all first-order anyway.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Here is the scope, stated plainly.

Supported: mixed and population only models, differential equations,
delay differential equations, closed form models, censoring, the
residual catalog, user written likelihoods, inter occasion
variability, and two component mixtures.

Refused, with an explanation rather than a silent approximation:
mixtures beyond two components for now, and the discrete
distributions.

The bridge is also deliberately first order, which rules out some
specialized Stan models.

:::

## If you already have an nlmixr2 model, you already have the Bayesian one

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```r
pak::pak("nlmixr2/nlmixr2bayes")
```

- Add `prior()` lines to `ini({})`
- Change `est="focei"` to `est="nuts"`
- That is the whole migration
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .checks}
- The posterior is sampled against the **identical** likelihood code
  your FOCEi run used
- "What does the Bayesian version say?" becomes a question about the
  data and the priors
- Not about whether you translated the model correctly
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
So, to close.

If you have an nlmixr2 model you already trust, adding
prior lines changes the model to a bayesian one.

Which means that, for the first time, when you ask what does the
Bayesian version say, you don't have to worry about your model being
translated correctly.
:::
